title: Laetare Sunday
hookLine: the rose vestments again, halfway through Lent

cards: Anyone who has run a long race knows the halfway marker. Your legs hurt, the excitement of the start line is gone, and the finish is still a long way off.
Then a water table, someone on the curb cheering, and you find a little more. Lent has one too. On its fourth Sunday, for one day, the violet gives way to rose.
If you were here back in Advent for Gaudete Sunday, you've seen this color before. It shows up only twice a year, and both times it means the same thing.

teach.b: Laetare is Latin for rejoice, said to one: to a city. It's the first word of the old entrance chant for the fourth Sunday of Lent, from the last chapter of Isaiah.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all you that love her."
Isaiah wrote to people who had mourned Jerusalem's ruin, promising that the city would be like a mother again, nursing and comforting her children.
The Church picked that verse for the middle of Lent, when the fasting starts to feel long, the resolutions are wobbling, and Easter is still out of sight. So for one day, the color lightens.
Flowers, usually left off the altar in Lent, may come back, and the organ can play more freely.

It's sometimes called Mid-Lent Sunday, and in England and Ireland it's also Mothering Sunday, when people once traveled to their mother church, the cathedral or the parish of their baptism; later it became a day to honor mothers too.
In some years the gospel is the prodigal son, with a feast for the one who came home. In others it's the man born blind, who sees.
Both are stories where the long darkness breaks. Rome kept a custom too: on this Sunday popes would bless a golden rose, an ornament of gold sometimes given to a church or a person as an honor.
Gaudete in Advent, Laetare in Lent: each time, the color tells the people in the pews how far they've already come.

how: On the fourth Sunday of Lent the priest may wear rose vestments instead of violet, and the entrance antiphon begins with Isaiah 66:10, Laetare, Jerusalem.

games.q: it's the fourth Sunday of Lent. you're preparing the church. what's allowed today that usually isn't in Lent?
o: rose vestments and flowers on the altar.
games.why: rose vestments and flowers may return. the Alleluia waits for Easter.

practice: Breathe in slowly, as if breathing in something good, fresh air, morning, the smell of rain, and breathe out whatever has felt heavy this Lent, a few times over.
Then name one thing you're honestly glad about today, however small, and let it be enough. If you pray, say Isaiah's word, rejoice; if not, let the gladness have a minute.

wordCard.voice: Laetare. Latin for rejoice; the fourth Sunday of Lent, halfway to Easter, with rose vestments. Today's word.
